# ParseDate

Reads a date written as an ISO 8601 string and gives it in the standard UTC form.

## Signature

```jyro
# fragment
ParseDate(text)
```

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `text` | string | The text to read: a string only. Any other type, null included, is a runtime error. |

## Returns

String. The instant text gives, in UTC to the millisecond, in the form `yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ss.fffZ`; null when text is not a date in one of the accepted forms.

## Remarks

The forms accepted here are the ones every date function accepts. A date is four digits of year, two of month and two of day, as in `2024-01-15`, and the day must exist in its month. It may be followed by `T` and a time of two digits each of hour, minute and second, as in `T09:30:00`; then, optionally, a point and one or more digits of fraction; then, optionally, `Z` or an offset of the form `+HH:mm` or `-HH:mm`. `T` and `Z` may be in either case. A date alone is midnight; a time with no offset is UTC. A second of 60 is read as 59, and a fraction is kept to the millisecond, its further digits discarded. A space in place of `T`, a time with no seconds, an offset with no colon, or any text before or after is not accepted, and neither is an instant before `0001-01-01T00:00:00.000Z` or after `9999-12-31T23:59:59.999Z`.

## Example

`ParseDate("2024-01-15T10:30:00+02:00")` returns `"2024-01-15T08:30:00.000Z"`.

`ParseDate("15/01/2024")` returns null.
